Neal is 58, works as software developer, unstable transitional.

How life is going overall. poor.

What brings them here now. Neal, 58, is a senior developer whose twenty-six-year marriage ended last autumn; since the house sold he has been living month-to-month in a room over a garage, and he reports going as long as eleven days without a conversation beyond work standups, with calls to his two adult children narrowed to logistics. He denies any decline in work performance, denies increased drinking, and denies thoughts of self-harm, framing the isolation as 'a logistics problem' to be scheduled back into order.
What they want out of support: By the end of this I want one regular thing a week where I'm actually with people — Thursday nights at Ed's table would do it — instead of talking myself out of it in the parking lot.

Predisposing. Neal grew up outside Millville in a house that ran on competence — his father a shift foreman at the glass works, his mother keeping the books for a lumber yard — where dinner was at six and the conversation was work, weather, and what needed fixing. When his grandfather died the spring Neal was twelve, the family went to the funeral, mowed his grandmother's lawn all summer, and never said the man's name in the house again. He learned that you handled things by handling them and that what you felt was your own business, and he carried that into a marriage where he showed up as gutters cleaned, bills paid, and a full oil tank.

Precipitating. Last October, after twenty-six years of marriage, Lynn told him she had felt like a roommate for the last decade of it; the divorce was final in February, and the house sold at the start of March. Since then he has been in a month-to-month room over a detached garage across town, staying at the office past seven because the room is worse than the desk. He cancelled five straight Thursday model-railroad nights — the layout used to fill his own basement and now sits in Ed's garage in pieces — stopped opening the Audubon walk emails, and let his daughter keep believing the house was still on the market. In April, after sitting twenty minutes in the car outside Ed's without going in, he counted it up the way he'd audit a failing system — eleven days since a conversation that wasn't about sprint tickets, two texts unanswered, one lunch declined — and called this service the next morning.

Perpetuating. Underneath, it is one strategy in three forms — carry it alone, keep it off everyone's desk, keep the hands busy — which protects the job and the pride while spending exactly the people still reaching toward him. The matchbooks settle him for the length of a task, never the length of a night.
- withdrawal: Five Thursdays running he has texted Ed some version of 'next week for sure,' and the Audubon walk emails sit unopened in a folder he named 'later'; at work he has taken to eating lunch at his desk with headphones on, which he tells himself is focus.
- hiding_needs: His daughter believes the house is still on the market — the room over the garage is 'a short-term thing between closings' — nobody at work knows about his feet, and the neurology appointments go on the shared calendar as 'dentist'; when anyone asks how he's doing he says 'can't complain,' and mostly believes it because he hasn't told anyone the rest.

Protective. Ed, the retired electrician he's laid track with every other Thursday for fifteen years, still texts that the table's clear and the layout's waiting, and hasn't stopped asking even after five cancellations. At work, two junior developers still bring him their broken builds before anyone else's, and he trusts that part of himself without question — give him a failing system and he will sit with it until it's sorted. The first week in the room he mounted a bird feeder outside the window and has logged twenty-three species from the chair beside it, which isn't the marsh at first light but keeps that patience in practice.
